title: Why $90 a month takes so long
hook: $3,000 owed, $90 paid every month. Simple division says 33 months. Does it?

knows: what interest on a debt is
doesNotKnow: that interest is charged on what is still owed each month, before the payment reduces the debt
that a payment close to the monthly interest barely shrinks the balance

misconception: $3,000 at $90 a month takes about 33 months (just divide the balance by the payment).
objective: The learner can explain that each month's interest is taken out of the payment first, so only the part above the interest pays down the debt, and a payment that only covers the interest never clears it.

claims.text: 20% a year is treated as 1.667% a month.
claims.source: 20% / 12 = 1.6667%. A simplification: real cards differ in how they compute interest (e.g. daily balances).

claims.text: In the first month the interest on $3,000 is $50, so a $90 payment takes only $40 off the debt.
Paying $90 a month, the $3,000 balance is cleared on the 50th payment (versus 33.3 months with no interest).
claims.source: n = −ln(1 − 3,000 × 0.016667 / 90) / ln(1.016667) = 0.8109 / 0.016529 = 49.06, so the 50th (partial) payment. Confirmed by stepping the balance month by month (Demo.tsx schedule()). 3,000 / 90 = 33.3.

claims.text: Paying $90 a month, the total interest is about $1,415.
At $50 a month the payment equals the monthly interest, so the balance never falls.
The stage's payoff times and interest totals for other payments come from the same month-by-month stepping (e.g. $150 a month: 25 months, about $680 interest).
claims.source: Demo.tsx schedule(): b ← b × 1.016667 − pay until b ≤ 0. At $150: 25 payments, interest 679.82.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: a fixed rate, interest added monthly, no fees, no new purchases.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation in Demo.tsx.

recall.question: A debt charges $60 interest a month. Which payment shrinks it twice as fast as $80?
recall.why: Interest is paid first. $80 takes $20 off the debt; $100 takes $40, twice as much (at first). What counts is the part above the interest.
